units.summary: One-dimensional arrays (declaring, subscripts, initialization, loops, range-based for, processing, parallel arrays, array parameters), plus an introduction to two-dimensional arrays and the STL vector.

lessons.title: Declaring arrays, subscripts, and no bounds checking
lessons.html:
The idea: one name for a row of values

Suppose a program needs the minutes you exercised on each day of a week. With ordinary variables you would need seven of them: day1, day2 and so on. That means seven statements to read them and seven more to print them. A loop cannot help, because a loop cannot step from one variable name to the next.

An array solves this. It is one variable that holds several values of the same type, stored side by side in memory. Picture a row of numbered boxes with one name on the whole row. Each box is an element. The number that picks out one box is its subscript (also called an index).

minutes:    30   45    0   60   20   15   40
subscript:   0    1    2    3    4    5    6

If you know Python, an array is like a list with three big differences. Its size is fixed when it is created and never changes (there is no append). Every element has the same type. And nothing checks that you stay inside it, which gets its own section below.

Defining an array

const int DAYS = 7;
int minutes[DAYS];    // 7 ints
double temps[24];     // 24 doubles
string names[5];      // 5 strings

A definition has three parts, always in this order: the element type, the array name, and the number of elements in square brackets. That number is called the size declarator. So double temps[24]; reads "temps is an array of 24 doubles".

The brackets go after the name. double[24] temps; does not compile. Watch out for parentheses too: double temps(24); does compile, but it is not an array. Parentheses after a variable name give it a starting value, so that line makes one double that holds 24.

How much memory? The elements sit next to each other, so an array uses the number of elements times the size of one element. On a system with 4-byte ints, int values[10]; uses 10 times 4 = 40 bytes, and sizeof(values) reports 40. The size declarator counts elements, not bytes.

Rules for the size declarator

The compiler works out how much room the array needs while it translates the program, before the program runs and before anyone types anything. So the size declarator must be a constant expression: a value the compiler can work out on its own. These qualify:

  • A literal: int d[10];
  • A named constant, meaning a const int set to a literal: const int M = 5; then int a[M];
  • Arithmetic built only from those: int b[M + 3]; makes 8 elements.

An ordinary variable does not qualify, even if it already holds a value:

int n;
cin >> n;
int c[n];      // NOT standard C++: n is not a constant

A warning about your compiler: g++ accepts int c[n]; as an extension (an extra feature that is not part of standard C++) and gives no warning, even with -Wall. So the code may run for you. On the test, the standard is the answer: a variable size is not allowed.

The size must also be greater than zero. int counts[-5]; is a compile error, because you cannot make minus five boxes. A size of zero is not allowed by the standard either.

Subscripts start at 0

To use one element, write the array name and a subscript in brackets: minutes[3]. The first element is subscript 0, not 1. So an array of N elements has subscripts 0 through N - 1. For int minutes[7]; the valid subscripts are 0 to 6, and minutes[6] is the last element.

Each element is an ordinary int variable that happens to live inside the array. You can assign to it, use it in arithmetic, print it, or read into it with cin. The subscript can be any integer expression: minutes[2], minutes[i], minutes[i + 1].

An array can get starting values from a list in braces, called an initialization list. The values go into the elements in order, starting at subscript 0. (The next lesson covers these lists in detail.) Here is a trace in which each line uses the values left by the line before it:

int v[4] = {5, 10, 15, 20};
v[0] = v[2] + 1;
v[3] = v[0] * 2;
v[1]++;
After the linev[0]v[1]v[2]v[3]
int v[4] = {5, 10, 15, 20};5101520
v[0] = v[2] + 1;16101520
v[3] = v[0] * 2;16101532
v[1]++;16111532

Two things to notice. The third line uses the new value of v[0], which is 16, because the second line already changed it. And v[2] keeps its 15 the whole time, because no line assigns to it.

When the brackets in a definition are empty, the compiler counts the list for you: int a[] = {15, 25, 35, 45, 55}; makes 5 elements. To find where a value lives, count from 0: 15 is at subscript 0, 25 at 1, 35 at 2, 45 at 3 and 55 at 4.

The number in brackets has two meanings

int a[5];    // definition: 5 is the size declarator
a[4] = 9;    // statement: 4 is a subscript, the last element
a[5] = 9;    // statement: 5 is a subscript, one PAST the end

In a definition the number says how many elements to make. Everywhere else it picks one element. So the same 5 means "five elements" on the first line and "the element after the last one" on the third.

Loops and arrays

Arrays and for loops go together, because the loop counter can serve as the subscript. This code reads four employees' hours and then prints them:

const int SIZE = 4;
int hours[SIZE];

for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++)
{
    cout << "Hours for employee " << (i + 1) << ": ";
    cin >> hours[i];
}
for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++)
    cout << hours[i] << " ";

Suppose the user enters 40, 35, 38 and 20. The first loop runs with i equal to 0, 1, 2 and 3, which are exactly the valid subscripts, so it fills hours[0] to hours[3]. When i becomes 4 the test 4 < 4 is false, and the loop stops before it touches anything outside the array. The second loop prints 40 35 38 20. The prompt shows i + 1 because people number employees from 1, while the array numbers them from 0.

Remember this pattern: start at 0 and test i < SIZE. It visits every element once and never leaves the array.

An array of numbers (such as int or double) defined inside a function, with no initialization list, starts out holding garbage: whatever bits were left in that memory. You cannot predict its values. Store a value in each element, with a loop or an initialization list, before you read it.

No bounds checking

C++ does not check that a subscript is inside the array. This is what "no bounds checking" means. Python stops with an IndexError if you go past the end of a list. C++ does not stop. It compiles the statement, and at run time it goes to the memory where that element would be if the array were longer, and reads or writes there.

int a[5];
a[5] = 9;     // compiles, then writes to memory past the array

That memory may belong to another variable. So the write can silently change a different variable, crash the program, or appear to do nothing at all. The C++ standard calls this undefined behavior: the language makes no promise about what happens, and the same program can act differently on another day or another computer. Reading out of range is just as bad: you get garbage or a crash.

A negative subscript is also out of range. In Python a[-1] is the last element. In C++ a[-1] is the memory just before the array. Keeping every subscript between 0 and size - 1 is your job, not the compiler's.

The off-by-one error

The most common way to leave an array is a loop that runs one time too many or one time too few. This is called an off-by-one error. Here are the two usual versions, for int a[6];:

for (int i = 0; i <= 6; i++)   // i is 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
    a[i] = 0;                  // 7 passes: last writes a[6]

for (int i = 1; i <= 6; i++)   // i is 1,2,3,4,5,6
    a[i] = 0;                  // a[0] never set, a[6] outside

Both compile, and both may seem to work. The fix is the pattern from above:

for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++)    // i is 0,1,2,3,4,5
    a[i] = 0;

A quick check: list the values the counter takes. They must start at 0, and there must be exactly as many of them as the array has elements.

An array name is not one value

The name alone, with no brackets, stands for the whole row, and C++ will not treat it as one value. b = a; does not compile. cout << a; prints a memory address (the place in memory where the array starts, shown in hexadecimal, a base-16 notation that uses the digits 0 to 9 and the letters a to f) such as 0x7ffd4b7546c0, not the values. a == b compiles, but it compares where the arrays sit in memory, so it is false even when every value matches. Work element by element with a loop instead. A later lesson in this unit shows how.

Mistakes students make

  • Thinking the last element of int a[8]; is a[8]. It is a[7].
  • Writing i <= SIZE in a loop test, or starting the counter at 1. Both are off-by-one errors.
  • Expecting the compiler or the running program to catch a bad subscript. Neither does.
  • Using a variable typed by the user as the size declarator. It is not standard C++, even though g++ accepts it.
  • Writing double sales(12); to make an array. That is one double holding 12.
  • Thinking the size declarator counts bytes. It counts elements. Memory is elements times the size of one element.
  • Using an old value in a trace after a line has already changed that element.
  • Trying to copy, print or compare a whole array with =, << or ==.

What to remember for the test

  • Definition form: type name[size]; for example double sales[12];.
  • The size declarator must be a constant expression greater than 0: a literal, a const int, or arithmetic on those.
  • N elements means subscripts 0 to N - 1. The first is [0], the last is [N - 1].
  • Memory used = number of elements times bytes per element.
  • In a definition the bracket number is the size. In a statement it is a subscript.
  • No bounds checking: an out-of-range subscript compiles and gives undefined behavior.
  • Loop pattern: for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++).

lessons.title: Initialization, char arrays, range-based for, structured bindings
lessons.book: Section 7.2 (pages 394 to 400), Section 7.4 (pages 404 to 408), and structured bindings in Section 7.5 (page 416)
lessons.html:
Giving an array its values when you define it

Defining an array and then assigning each element in a separate statement is slow to write. An initialization list gives all the starting values in one line. The values go inside braces, separated by commas, and they fill the elements in order, starting at subscript 0.

int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
// a[0] is 10, a[1] is 20, a[2] is 30, a[3] is 40, a[4] is 50

There are four forms to know.

1. A full list. One value per element, as above.

2. Implicit sizing. Leave the brackets empty and the compiler counts the list and makes that many elements.

int b[] = {3, 6, 9};          // 3 elements
double rates[] = {1.5, 2.5};  // 2 elements

3. Partial initialization. If the list has fewer values than the array has elements, the listed values fill the front, and every element without a value is set to zero. For an int that is 0, for a double it is 0.0, and for a string it is the empty string "".

int c[6] = {4, 8};
string names[3] = {"Ann"};
Element[0][1][2][3][4][5]
c480000

names[0] is "Ann", and names[1] and names[2] are both the empty string. So a loop that prints each element of names inside brackets shows [Ann][][]. An empty string prints nothing, so its brackets close at once.

4. Empty braces. int d[4] = {}; has a list with no values in it, so every element is set to 0. This is the quick way to start an array at all zeros.

What an initialization list cannot do

Each of these is a compile error. Examiners like them.

CodeWhy it fails
int a[3] = {1, 2, 3, 4};More values than elements. A list can be shorter than the array, never longer.
int nums[6] = {2, 4, , 8};A gap. You cannot skip an element. The values always fill from the front, so there is also no way to set only the back elements.
int h[3] = 8, 12, 16;No braces. The values of an array must be inside braces.
double r[];No size and no list, so the compiler has nothing to count.
int a[3]; then later a = {1, 2, 3};A list works only in the definition. Later, assign one element at a time.

Arrays with no list at all

What an array holds when it has no initialization list depends on where it is defined.

  • A global array, defined outside all functions, starts with every element set to 0, just like a global variable. int g[3]; above main holds 0 0 0.
  • A local array, defined inside a function, holds garbage: leftover values you cannot predict. This applies to arrays of int, double and char. A string array is the exception: every string starts as the empty string "" wherever it is defined.

The zero-filling of partial initialization needs a list. Even {} or a single value is enough to make the rest 0. No list at all, inside a function, means garbage.

Character arrays and the null character

Before the string type existed, C++ (and the older language C) stored text in an array of char. Text stored this way is called a C-string. There is a problem to solve: the array may be bigger than the text in it, so how does the code know where the text stops? The answer is a marker. Right after the last real character sits the null character, written '\0'. Its ASCII code is 0. It is not the digit '0' (code 48) and it is not a space.

A string literal in double quotes always gets a null character added at the end:

char w[] = "plum";
subscript:   0    1    2    3    4
w:          'p'  'l'  'u'  'm'  '\0'

Four letters need five elements. The letter 'm' is at subscript 3, and w[4] holds the null.

  • char w[3] = "cat"; is a compile error. "cat" needs 4 elements: c, a, t and the null.
  • char name[10] = "Al"; is fine. It holds 'A' and 'l', and the partial rule sets the other 8 elements to '\0'.

cout and char arrays. In the last lesson you saw that cout << an int array prints a memory address. A char array is the exception: cout << w; prints characters starting at w[0] and stops when it reaches a '\0'. So it prints plum.

The trap. A list of single characters in braces adds no null:

char word[] = {'H', 'i'};   // 2 elements: 'H' 'i'
cout << word;               // no '\0' to stop at

cout prints H and i, then keeps reading the memory after the array until it happens to find a zero byte. That is undefined behavior. It may print junk characters after Hi, or it may happen to print just Hi, but nothing guarantees either. The fix is char word[] = "Hi";, which makes 3 elements including the null, or {'H', 'i', '\0'}.

The range-based for loop

Many loops over an array only need each value in turn. The range-based for loop does exactly that, with no subscript, no size and no chance of an off-by-one error. It works like Python's for x in scores:.

for (type rangeVariable : array)
    statement;

The variable before the colon is the range variable. On each pass it receives the next element, starting with element 0. Note that a colon separates the two parts, not a semicolon.

int scores[3] = {90, 75, 82};
for (int s : scores)
    cout << s << " ";        // prints 90 75 82

Pass 1: s is 90. Pass 2: s is 75. Pass 3: s is 82. Then the loop ends by itself, because it knows the array has 3 elements. You can write auto as the type: for (auto val : scores). As you saw earlier in the course, auto tells the compiler to pick the type itself, here the element type int.

The range variable is a copy

This is the point most tested. A plain range variable holds a copy of the element, so changing it changes only the copy.

int n[3] = {1, 2, 3};
for (int x : n)
    x = x * 10;         // changes the copy only
Passx starts asx after x = x * 10Array n
11 (copy of n[0])101 2 3
22 (copy of n[1])201 2 3
33 (copy of n[2])301 2 3

The array never changes. To change the elements, make the range variable a reference by writing & before its name. A reference is another name for an existing variable, the same idea as a reference parameter in the functions unit. Now x is each element in turn.

for (int &x : n)
    x = x * 10;         // n becomes 10 20 30

When you need a regular counting loop instead. A range-based for loop gives you values but never their subscripts. If the subscript matters, use for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++). Examples: copying a[i] into the same position b[i] of another array, printing "Element 2 is 75", or working on only part of an array. Displaying, adding up, or doubling every element (with &) do not need subscripts.

One limit: the range-based for loop needs an array whose size the compiler knows. It does not work on an array that was passed into a function as a parameter. Lesson 5 of this unit explains why.

Structured binding declarations (C++17)

A structured binding declaration unpacks a small array into separately named variables in one line. It starts with auto, and the new names go in square brackets.

int p[3] = {7, 8, 9};
auto [x, y, z] = p;    // x is 7, y is 8, z is 9
y = y + 100;           // y is 108, p[1] is still 8

Two rules:

  • The number of names must equal the number of elements exactly. auto [x, y] = p; for a 3-element array is a compile error. C++ does not drop the extra value.
  • The new variables hold copies. Changing y leaves p[1] alone.

It is like Python's x, y, z = p, except that a wrong count is caught when the program compiles, not when it runs.

Mistakes students make

  • Thinking a partial list leaves the remaining elements as garbage. They become 0, 0.0 or "".
  • Giving more values than the size declarator allows, or leaving a gap in the list.
  • Assigning a list to an array after its definition: a = {1, 2, 3};.
  • Forgetting the null character when counting the elements of char w[] = "plum";. It has 5.
  • Filling a char array with {'H', 'i'} and then printing it with cout.
  • Expecting for (int x : a) x *= 2; to change the array. It needs int &x.
  • Writing a semicolon instead of the colon in a range-based for header.
  • Listing the wrong number of names in a structured binding.

What to remember for the test

  • A list fills from subscript 0. Fewer values: the rest become zero. More values: compile error.
  • int b[] = {3, 6, 9}; has 3 elements. int d[4] = {}; is all zeros.
  • No list: global arrays are all 0, local arrays hold garbage.
  • A C-string ends with '\0', the null character, ASCII 0. A literal with n letters needs n + 1 elements.
  • for (type v : array): v is a copy. Use type &v to change the elements.
  • Use a counting loop when you need the subscript.
  • auto [a, b, c] = arr; needs exactly one name per element and makes copies.

lessons.title: Processing array contents
lessons.html:
The idea: a loop plus a pattern

Almost every job you do with an array is a loop that visits the elements, plus a few lines that do something with each one. This lesson is a toolbox of those patterns: totals and averages, highest and lowest, counting, searching, copying and comparing, and arrays that are only partly full. For each pattern, learn two things: which variables are set up before the loop, and with what starting value, and what the loop does with each element.

Changing one element: where the ++ goes

Each element is an ordinary variable, so ++ and -- work on it. Recall from the loops unit: x++ (postfix) uses the old value, then adds 1, while ++x (prefix) adds 1 first and uses the new value. With arrays there is one more question: is the operator on the element or on the subscript?

CodeWhat changes
a[k]++ or a[k]--The element a[k] goes up or down by 1. k is unchanged.
a[k++] or a[k--]a[k] is used with the old k, then k changes. The ++ or -- changes no element.
++a[k]The element goes up by 1 first, and the new value is used.

The rule: an operator inside the brackets changes the subscript variable. An operator outside the brackets changes the element.

int e[] = {3, 6, 9};
int k = 0;
e[k]++;            // e is {4, 6, 9}, k is still 0
int v = e[k++];    // v = e[0], which is 4. Then k becomes 1.
                   // e is unchanged: {4, 6, 9}
cout << ++e[2];    // e[2] becomes 10 first, so this prints 10

Totals and averages

An accumulator is a variable that starts at 0 and has each element added to it in turn.

const int SIZE = 4;
int nums[SIZE] = {7, 3, 6, 9};
int total = 0;                     // must start at 0
for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++)
    total += nums[i];
double avg = static_cast<double>(total) / SIZE;
inums[i]total after the pass
070 + 7 = 7
137 + 3 = 10
2610 + 6 = 16
3916 + 9 = 25

Now the average. total / SIZE is 25 / 4 with two ints, which is integer division: the fraction is dropped and the result is 6. To get 6.25, at least one side must be a double: 25 / 4.0 or static_cast<double>(total) / SIZE.

Two traps. First, total must start at 0. A local variable with no starting value holds garbage. Second, if you total a second array with the same variable, set total = 0; again before the second loop. Otherwise the second total still contains the first: if the first array gave 25 and the second array's values add to 10, you get 35.

Highest and lowest

Keep a variable that holds the highest value seen so far. Start it with the first element, then compare every other element against it.

int s[] = {70, 95, 60, 95, 80};
int hi = s[0], pos = 0;
for (int i = 1; i < 5; i++)
    if (s[i] > hi)
    {
        hi = s[i];
        pos = i;     // remember where it was
    }
is[i]s[i] > hi?hipos
start700
19595 > 70 yes951
26060 > 95 no951
39595 > 95 no951
48080 > 95 no951

Ties. Look at i = 3. The second 95 is equal to hi, not greater, so it does not replace it. With > the first of several equal highest values keeps its position (here 1). If the test were >=, an equal value would pass, and the last one would win (pos would end at 3).

Why start with s[0] and not 0? The lowest value uses the same pattern with <: int lo = s[0]; then if (s[i] < lo) lo = s[i];. That gives 60. Suppose you started with lo = 0 instead. Every element here is positive, so none is less than 0. lo never changes, and the program reports 0, which is not even in the array. Starting hi at 0 fails the same way when every value is negative. Starting with the first element guarantees the starting value really is in the array. Because element 0 is already counted, the loop can begin at 1.

Counting

A counter starts at 0 and goes up by 1 each time a test is true. To count the scores of 80 or more in s:

int count = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
    if (s[i] >= 80)
        count++;          // 95, 95 and 80 pass, so count is 3

The same pattern counts how many positions differ between two arrays: if (a[i] != b[i]) diff++;.

Searching

A linear search looks at the elements one by one until it finds the value it wants, called the target. The position starts at -1, which means "not found yet". -1 works as a marker because it can never be a real subscript.

int codes[] = {31, 54, 20, 54};
int target = 54, pos = -1, i = 0;
while (i < 4 && pos == -1)
{
    if (codes[i] == target)
        pos = i;
    i++;
}
Passi at startcodes[i]Match?pos afteri after
1031no-11
2154yes12

Now the test pos == -1 is false, so the loop stops. pos is 1 and i is 2. Notice that i is one past the match, because i++ still runs at the end of the pass that found it. The second 54 is never looked at: this search finds the first match. If the target is not in the array, every pass fails, the loop ends when i reaches 4, and pos stays -1.

Copying and comparing two arrays

An array name with no brackets stands for the memory address where the array begins. That explains three things you cannot do directly:

  • cout << scores; prints that address, a hexadecimal number such as 0x7ffd4b7546c0, not the values. (A char array holding a C-string is the exception: cout prints its text.)
  • dst = src; does not compile. C++ will not assign one array to another.
  • if (a == b) compiles, but it asks whether the two arrays start at the same address. Two different arrays never do, so it is false even when every value matches. g++ even warns about it.

Do both jobs element by element:

for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++)     // copy
    dst[i] = src[i];

bool same = true;                  // compare
for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++)
    if (a[i] != b[i])
        same = false;

Note that dst[8] = src[8]; is not a copy of the array. It copies one element, and for an 8-element array subscript 8 is past the end.

Shifting values inside one array

When a loop moves values within the same array, the direction matters, because each pass may read a value that an earlier pass already overwrote.

int a[4] = {6, 7, 8, 9};
for (int i = 1; i < 4; i++)
    a[i] = a[i - 1];
PassStatementArray after
i = 1a[1] = a[0], which is 66 6 8 9
i = 2a[2] = a[1], which is now 66 6 6 9
i = 3a[3] = a[2], which is now 66 6 6 6

The first value spreads across the whole array. To shift every value one place to the right, run the loop backwards so each value is read before it is overwritten: for (int i = 3; i > 0; i--) a[i] = a[i - 1]; gives 6 6 7 8.

Partially filled arrays

Often you do not know how many values there will be. The size of an array must be a constant, so you define the array for the largest number you might need and keep a separate int that says how many elements are really in use. This is a partially filled array. The count also tells you the next free subscript.

Here the user types numbers and ends with -1. A value like this, which means "no more data", is a sentinel. It is tested for but not stored.

const int MAX = 100;
int data[MAX];
int count = 0;
int v;
cin >> v;
while (v != -1 && count < MAX)
{
    data[count] = v;
    count++;
    cin >> v;
}

Trace with the input 12 5 30 -1:

vTestBody doescount after
12truedata[0] = 12, reads 51
5truedata[1] = 5, reads 302
30truedata[2] = 30, reads -13
-1falsenothing, the loop ends3

The test count < MAX matters. Without it, a user who typed more than 100 values would make the program store past the end of the array, and C++ would not stop it.

From now on, every loop over this array runs to count, not to MAX: for (int i = 0; i < count; i++). The elements from count onward were never given values. Running to MAX shows garbage, and i <= count shows one garbage element. To go backwards, start at the last used element: for (int i = count - 1; i >= 0; i--) prints 30 5 12.

Two shorter forms you will see. data[count++] = v; stores at the current count, then adds 1 to it, because the postfix ++ is inside the brackets. And cin >> v can be used as a condition: it reads a value and counts as true if the read worked. Combined:

while (count < MAX && cin >> v && v != -1)
    data[count++] = v;

Mistakes students make

  • Not starting an accumulator or counter at 0, or not resetting it before a second array.
  • Dividing two ints for an average and losing the fraction.
  • Starting a highest or lowest search at 0 instead of the first element.
  • Mixing up > and >= when there are ties: first match versus last match.
  • Reading a[k--] as changing the element. It changes k.
  • Using =, == or cout << on whole arrays.
  • Shifting in the wrong direction and copying one value everywhere.
  • Looping to the array size, or to <= count, in a partially filled array.
  • Leaving out count < MAX when filling an array from input.

What to remember for the test

  • Accumulators and counters start at 0. Highest and lowest start at element 0.
  • int / int drops the fraction. Make one side a double for a true average.
  • > keeps the first of equal values. >= keeps the last.
  • Search: pos starts at -1. Stopping at the first match leaves i one past it.
  • An array name alone is an address. Copy and compare with a loop.
  • Partially filled array: loop i < count. Fill with a count < MAX test. The sentinel is not stored.
  • For any trace, write the array out and update it after every statement.

lessons.title: Parallel arrays
lessons.html:
The idea: one subscript, several arrays

Often each item in your data has more than one piece of information. A shop item has a name, a price and a stock count. A student has a name and a score. One array can hold only one type, so a single array cannot store both a string name and an int score.

The answer is to use one array for each piece of information, and to agree that the same subscript means the same item in every array. Arrays used this way are called parallel arrays.

const int N = 4;
string item[N]  = {"pen", "pad", "ink", "tape"};
double cost[N]  = {1.25, 3.50, 7.00, 2.75};
int    stock[N] = {40, 12, 0, 25};

Picture a table. Each array is a column and each subscript is a row:

Subscriptitemcoststock
0pen1.2540
1pad3.5012
2ink7.000
3tape2.7525

Row 2 is the ink: item[2], cost[2] and stock[2] all describe it. If you know Python, this is like keeping a list of names and a list of scores and always using names[i] together with scores[i].

Three facts follow from the definition:

  • The arrays may have different types. Here they are string, double and int. What they must share is the number of elements and the order of the items.
  • C++ does not know the arrays are related. To the compiler they are three separate arrays. The link exists only in how your code uses the subscripts.
  • "Parallel" says nothing about memory. The arrays are not stored in any special place. And parallel arrays are not an array with two subscripts. That is a two-dimensional array, which comes later in this unit.

One loop, one subscript

To work through the items, use a single subscript variable for every array. Each pass then deals with one whole row. This loop lists the items that are low on stock:

for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    if (stock[i] < 20)
        cout << item[i] << " " << stock[i] << endl;
istock[i]stock[i] < 20?Prints
040no
112yespad 12
20yesink 0
325no

The test looks at one array, and the output uses the same i in another. Because the subscript is shared, each item is printed beside its own stock count.

Filling parallel arrays from input works the same way. If each line the user types holds a name and a score:

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
    cin >> name[i] >> score[i];

Each pass stores one name and its score at the same subscript, so they stay paired.

Finding the best item: keep the subscript

To find the most expensive item, you need more than the highest price. You also need to know which item it belongs to. So keep the subscript of the best item so far, not its value.

int best = 0;                      // a subscript
for (int i = 1; i < N; i++)
    if (cost[i] > cost[best])
        best = i;
cout << item[best] << " " << cost[best];
iComparisonbest after
start0 (cost 1.25)
13.50 > 1.25 yes1
27.00 > 3.50 yes2
32.75 > 7.00 no2

best ends at 2, so the program prints item[2] and cost[2]: ink 7. (A double holding 7.00 prints as 7 unless you format it.) Had you stored only the price 7.00, you could not get back to the name. With the subscript you can reach every array.

Looking up one item

To answer "what does the tape cost?", search one array for the item, remember the subscript where it was found, then use that subscript in the other array.

string want = "tape";
int found = -1;                  // -1 means not found
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    if (item[i] == want)
        found = i;
if (found != -1)
    cout << cost[found];         // prints 2.75
else
    cout << "not found";

The loop finds "tape" at subscript 3, so found becomes 3 and cost[3], 2.75, is printed. Two things to notice:

  • This loop does not stop at a match. It checks every element, so if the value appeared twice, found would end with the last match. With only one match, that makes no difference.
  • Always check for -1 before using the subscript. If the item is missing, found stays -1, and cost[-1] is outside the array: undefined behavior.

Rearranging: change every array the same way

Because C++ does not know the arrays are linked, it will not keep them in step for you. Suppose you swap the first two items. Swapping two elements needs a temporary variable to hold one value while the other moves:

string t = item[0];
item[0] = item[1];
item[1] = t;          // item is now: pad pen ink tape

Now look at the rows. cost was not touched, so it is still 1.25, 3.50, 7.00, 2.75.

Subscriptitemcost
0pad1.25 (the pen's price)
1pen3.50 (the pad's price)

The program compiles and runs without any error, but two items now show the wrong cost. Any reordering, a swap or a full sort, must be repeated in every parallel array, using the same subscripts. Later in the course you will meet classes, which keep all of one item's data together in a single object, so the pieces cannot get out of step.

Mistakes students make

  • Thinking parallel arrays must have the same type. They only need the same number of elements, in the same order.
  • Confusing parallel arrays with a two-dimensional array (one array, two subscripts).
  • Keeping the best value instead of the best subscript, and then not knowing which name goes with it.
  • Using different subscripts for the arrays inside one loop.
  • Rearranging one array and forgetting the others.
  • Using a "found" subscript without first checking that it is not -1.

What to remember for the test

  • Parallel arrays: two or more arrays where the same subscript holds data about the same item.
  • Types may differ. The link is the subscript.
  • C++ knows nothing about the link. Swap or sort one array, and you must do the same to all.
  • To find something, search one array for its subscript, then use that subscript in the others.
  • To trace, write the arrays as columns of a table and read across the row.

lessons.title: Arrays as function arguments
lessons.book: Section 7.7, pages 420 to 430, and the case study in Section 7.10, pages 440 to 441
lessons.html:
The idea: the function gets the address, not a copy

In the functions unit you met two ways to pass an argument. By value: the parameter is a copy, so the function cannot change the caller's variable. By reference (with &): the parameter is another name for the caller's variable, so changes are real.

Arrays work differently from both. When you pass an array, C++ does not copy its elements. It passes the memory address of the first element, which tells the function where the caller's array lives. The function then reaches the caller's own elements through that address. Think of handing someone the address of your storage unit rather than a copy of everything inside it. If they rearrange the boxes, your unit is rearranged. So the effect is the same as passing by reference: the function works on the original array, even though you write no &.

Three results follow, and the rest of this lesson is about them:

  1. A function can change the caller's array.
  2. Passing an array is fast, even a huge one, because nothing is copied.
  3. The function does not know how many elements the array has. An address says where the array starts, not how long it is. So the size is passed as a separate argument.

Writing the function and the call

void show(const int a[], int n)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        cout << a[i] << " ";
    cout << endl;
}

int main()
{
    int v[4] = {5, 6, 7, 8};
    show(v, 4);          // prints 5 6 7 8
    return 0;
}
  • The parameter is the type, the name, then empty brackets: int a[]. No size goes in the brackets, because the parameter only receives an address. (The const in front is explained below.)
  • The size is its own parameter with its own type: int n.
  • The call uses the array's name alone, with no brackets: show(v, 4).
  • A prototype may leave out the parameter names but must keep the brackets: void show(const int[], int);

These look close but are wrong:

WrongWhy
void show(int a[], n)n has no type. Every parameter needs one.
void show(int[] a, int n)The brackets go after the name, not after the type. (That is Java's style.)
void show(const int a, int n)No brackets, so a is a single int. Passing an array to it will not compile.
show(v[], 4);Brackets never appear after the name in a call.
show(v[4], 4);v[4] is one element (here one past the end), not the array. It will not compile.
show(int v[], 4);Types are written in definitions and headers, never in a call.

The function changes the caller's array

void bump(int a[], int n)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        a[i] *= 2;
}

If v holds 5 6 7 8 and main calls bump(v, 4);, then inside bump the name a reaches the same four elements as v. Pass 0 doubles v[0] to 10, pass 1 doubles v[1] to 12, and so on. Back in main, v holds 10 12 14 16.

Compare passing one element:

void setOne(int x) { x = 0; }

setOne(v[0]);     // v[0] is unchanged

v[0] is a single int, and a single int passed to an ordinary int parameter is passed by value. x is a copy, so setting it to 0 does nothing to v[0].

CallWhat the function receivesCan it change the caller's data?
bump(v, 4) to int a[]The address of v[0]Yes, any element
setOne(v[0]) to int xA copy of one intNo

So the statement "arrays are passed by value" is false.

Swapping elements inside a function

To swap two elements, hold one in a temporary variable while the other moves. This function reverses an array by swapping the first with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on. For subscript i, its partner at the other end is n - 1 - i.

void reverse(int a[], int n)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < n / 2; i++)
    {
        int t = a[i];
        a[i] = a[n - 1 - i];
        a[n - 1 - i] = t;
    }
}

With {2, 4, 6, 8} and n = 4, the loop runs while i < 2:

iSwapsArray after
start2 4 6 8
0a[0] and a[3]8 4 6 2
1a[1] and a[2]8 6 4 2

Only half as many passes as elements are needed, because each pass fixes two positions. If n is odd, n / 2 uses integer division and rounds down, so the middle element is never touched, which is right: it is already in place. Because the function works on the caller's array, the caller sees the reversed values.

const: a promise not to change the array

Since a function can change the caller's array, a function that only needs to read it should promise not to. Put the keyword const before the parameter's type: const int a[]. The compiler then enforces the promise. Any statement that assigns to an element is a compile error:

void clear(const int a[], int n)
{
    a[0] = 0;     // error: a is read-only
}

The program never gets to run, so no element is changed. Use const for every function that displays, totals, searches or compares an array.

The function does not know the size

The parameter holds only a starting address. Nothing there says how many elements follow, so:

  • The caller must pass the size, and the function trusts it.
  • A range-based for loop on the parameter does not compile, because that loop needs to know where the array ends. Neither does a structured binding. Use a counting loop up to the size parameter instead.
  • The caller can pass a smaller size on purpose. The function then works on only the first that many elements. This is how you pass a partially filled array: pass its count.
int total(const int a[], int n)
{
    int t = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        t += a[i];
    return t;
}

int w[] = {2, 4, 6, 8};
cout << total(w, 4);    // 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20
cout << total(w, 2);    // only w[0] and w[1]: 2 + 4 = 6

Functions that return a result about an array

A function cannot return a whole array as its return value. It can return something worked out from the array: a total, the lowest value, a count, the subscript of the highest element, or a bool answer.

bool allPositive(const int a[], int n)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        if (a[i] <= 0)
            return false;    // stop at the first bad value
    return true;             // reached only if none was bad
}

With {4, -1, 7} and n = 3: at i = 0, 4 is fine. At i = 1, -1 fails the test, and return false ends the function at once. With n = 1, only the 4 is checked, the loop finishes, and the function returns true. The pattern to remember: return false inside the loop, return true after it. Writing else return true; inside the loop is a bug, because the function would then decide after looking at only the first element.

Functions can also work together. To average a set of test scores after dropping the lowest one, a program can call one function for the total and another for the lowest, then divide by one fewer than the number of scores:

double s[4] = {70, 85, 100, 90};
double avg = (total(s, 4) - lowest(s, 4)) / 3;
// (345 - 70) / 3 = 275 / 3 = 91.6667

Here total and lowest are versions written for double arrays. lowest uses the lowest-value pattern from lesson 3: start with s[0] and replace it with any smaller element.

How cout shows the results

  • A bool prints as 1 for true and 0 for false.
  • A double prints with at most 6 significant digits by default, rounded, and without trailing zeros. 275.0 / 3 shows as 91.6667, 2.5 as 2.5, and 4.0 as 4.

Mistakes students make

  • Thinking arrays are passed by value and that the function works on a copy.
  • Thinking passing one element, f(v[0]), lets the function change it. A single int is copied.
  • Writing brackets or types in the call: show(v[], 4), show(v[4], 4), show(int v[], 4).
  • Leaving the type off the size parameter, or writing int[] a.
  • Forgetting the size parameter, or expecting the function to work out the size.
  • Using a range-based for loop on an array parameter.
  • Assigning to an element of a const array parameter.
  • Returning true too early from a check-every-element function.

What to remember for the test

  • Header: void f(const int a[], int n). Call: f(arr, size). Prototype: void f(const int[], int);
  • The function receives the address of the first element. Changes to a[i] change the caller's array.
  • const before the type makes the array read-only. Changing it is a compile error.
  • The function only knows the size you pass. A smaller size means it uses only the first elements.
  • No range-based for loop and no structured binding on an array parameter.
  • bool prints 1 or 0. A double prints up to 6 significant digits.

lessons.title: Two-dimensional arrays
lessons.html:
The idea: a table of values

A one-dimensional array is a single row of boxes. Some data is naturally a table: the scores of 3 students on 4 tests, the sales of 5 stores in each of 12 months. A two-dimensional array holds a table. Each element is reached with two subscripts: one picks the row, the other picks the column. If you know Python, this is like a list of lists, and grid[r][c] means the same thing.

const int ROWS = 3;
const int COLS = 4;
int scores[ROWS][COLS];    // 3 rows, 4 columns

The first size declarator is the number of rows and the second is the number of columns. Both follow the usual rules: constant, and greater than 0. The array has rows times columns elements, here 3 times 4 = 12, all of the same type.

Here is where each element sits. Row subscripts run 0 to 2 and column subscripts run 0 to 3:

col 0col 1col 2col 3
row 0[0][0][0][1][0][2][0][3]
row 1[1][0][1][1][1][2][1][3]
row 2[2][0][2][1][2][2][2][3]

Subscripts: row first, then column

Write name[row][column], each subscript in its own brackets. scores[1][3] = 88; stores 88 in row 1, column 3: the second student's fourth test. The two subscripts together name one element. A memory aid: read a table by going down to the row, then across to the column.

  • Both subscripts start at 0, so the last element of scores[3][4] is scores[2][3].
  • scores[2, 3] is not a way to write two subscripts. Always use two separate pairs of brackets.
  • There is still no bounds checking, in either direction.

Initializing a two-dimensional array

One inner list per row. Each pair of inner braces fills one row, starting at column 0.

int m[2][3] = {{7, 8, 9}, {1, 2, 3}};
// row 0: 7 8 9
// row 1: 1 2 3

One flat list. Without inner braces, the values fill the table in row order: all of row 0, then all of row 1. This gives the same table as above:

int n[2][3] = {7, 8, 9, 1, 2, 3};

Short lists. The zero rule from one-dimensional arrays still holds: elements that get no value become 0. But where the zeros land depends on the braces. Each inner list starts a new row, so a short row is padded with zeros, and its values never spill into the next row. A flat list just fills from the front.

int p[2][3] = {{4}, {5, 6}};   // row 0: 4 0 0   row 1: 5 6 0
int f[2][3] = {4, 5, 6, 7};    // row 0: 4 5 6   row 1: 7 0 0

Nested loops visit every element

To go through a table, put one loop inside another. Usually the outer loop walks the rows and the inner loop walks the columns. For each single pass of the outer loop, the inner loop runs all the way through.

int g[3][2];
for (int r = 0; r < 3; r++)
    for (int c = 0; c < 2; c++)
        g[r][c] = 10 * r + c;
rcStatement
00g[0][0] = 0
01g[0][1] = 1
10g[1][0] = 10
11g[1][1] = 11
20g[2][0] = 20
21g[2][1] = 21

The inner statement runs 3 times 2 = 6 times, once per element. When a question asks about one element of a table filled by a formula, you do not need to fill the whole table. Put that element's subscripts into the formula: g[2][1] is 10 times 2 + 1 = 21. Take care to use the row for r and the column for c.

To print the table as a grid, print one row in the inner loop, then end the line after the inner loop finishes:

for (int r = 0; r < 3; r++)
{
    for (int c = 0; c < 2; c++)
        cout << g[r][c] << " ";
    cout << endl;              // after each row
}

Totals: the whole table, each row, each column

Use this table of points for three players over three rounds:

int pts[3][3] = {{8, 6, 9},
                 {7, 7, 5},
                 {10, 4, 6}};

Whole table. Set the accumulator to 0 once, before both loops, and add every element: the total is 62.

Each row. Set the accumulator to 0 inside the outer loop, just before the inner loop, so each row starts fresh. Print it after the inner loop.

for (int r = 0; r < 3; r++)
{
    int sum = 0;                 // reset for each row
    for (int c = 0; c < 3; c++)
        sum += pts[r][c];
    cout << sum << " ";          // prints 23 19 20
}

Row 0 is 8 + 6 + 9 = 23, row 1 is 7 + 7 + 5 = 19, row 2 is 10 + 4 + 6 = 20. If sum = 0 were placed before the outer loop instead, it would never reset, and the printed totals would be 23 42 62.

Each column. Swap the roles of the loops: the outer loop walks the columns and the inner loop walks the rows. The element is still written pts[r][c], row first.

for (int c = 0; c < 3; c++)
{
    int sum = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < 3; r++)
        sum += pts[r][c];
    cout << sum << " ";          // prints 25 17 20
}

Where you reset the accumulator decides what you total.

Giving a 2D array to a function

As with a one-dimensional array, the function receives the address of the first element, so it works on the caller's table, and you pass the number of rows separately. The difference: the parameter must state the number of columns. Only the first brackets may be empty.

const int COLS = 3;      // global, so main and the function can use it

void showTable(const int t[][COLS], int rows)
{
    for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
    {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++)
            cout << t[r][c] << " ";
        cout << endl;
    }
}

showTable(pts, 3);       // the call: the name alone

Why the column size is needed. Memory is one long line, so the table is stored one row after another: row 0, then row 1, then row 2.

pts in memory:   8 6 9 | 7 7 5 | 10 4 6
                 row 0   row 1   row 2

To find t[2][1], the compiler skips 2 whole rows and then 1 more element. It can only skip a row if it knows how long a row is, which is the number of columns. It never needs the number of rows to find an element, which is why that one may be left out.

ParameterOK?
int t[][4], int rowsYes. Column size given, rows passed separately.
int t[][], int rowsNo. The column size is missing.
int t[4][], int rowsNo. A size is given for the rows, which is optional, but the required column size is missing.
int t[], int rows, 4No. A bare number is not a parameter.

Three or more dimensions

C++ allows as many dimensions as you need. Each one adds a size declarator, a subscript and a level of nested loop. int seats[2][3][4]; could be 2 floors of 3 rows of 4 seats: 2 times 3 times 4 = 24 elements, and seats[1][2][3] is the last one. As a parameter, every size except the first must be given: int s[][3][4]. You will rarely need more than two.

Mistakes students make

  • Reversing the subscripts: the first is the row, the second is the column.
  • Adding the two sizes instead of multiplying to count the elements.
  • Writing grid[2, 3] instead of grid[2][3].
  • Expecting a short inner list to spill into the next row. It is padded with zeros instead.
  • Resetting a row total in the wrong place, so it keeps running from row to row.
  • Leaving out the column size in a parameter: int t[][].

What to remember for the test

  • type name[ROWS][COLS]; has ROWS times COLS elements.
  • name[r][c]: row first, column second, each from 0.
  • Inner braces fill one row each. A flat list fills in row order. Missing elements are 0.
  • Outer loop on rows, inner loop on columns. Swap them for column totals.
  • Parameter: int t[][COLS], int rows. Every size except the first is required.
  • Three or more dimensions are allowed, one subscript per dimension.

lessons.title: Introduction to the STL vector
lessons.html:
The idea: an array that can grow

Arrays have three weak points you met in this unit. Their size is fixed before the program runs. When you do not know how many values are coming, you have to keep a separate count. And nothing checks the subscripts. The vector fixes the first two problems and offers a checked way to reach elements, which helps with the third.

A vector comes from the Standard Template Library (STL), a collection of ready-made data types and algorithms that comes with every C++ compiler. The STL's data types for holding many values are called containers, and they come in two kinds:

  • Sequence containers keep their elements in order, and you reach an element by its position, as with an array.
  • Associative containers find an element by a key, the way you look up a word in a dictionary. (A Python dict works this way.)

A vector keeps its elements in order and you reach them by position, so it is a sequence container. If you know Python, a vector is close to a Python list: it grows and shrinks and knows its own size. Unlike a Python list, it still holds only one type.

Defining a vector

Add #include <vector>. Most STL containers have their own header (<list> and <array> are for other containers). When you define a vector, put the element type in angle brackets after the word vector:

vector<int> a;               // empty: no elements, size 0
vector<int> b(5);            // 5 elements, all 0
vector<int> c(4, 7);         // 4 elements, all 7
vector<int> d = {2, 4, 6};   // 3 elements: 2 4 6
vector<int> e = {5};         // 1 element: 5
  • Parentheses set the size. Braces list the values. b(5) is five elements, each 0. {5} is one element holding 5. This is the easiest trap in the topic.
  • A vector's elements always start with a value: 0 for numbers unless you give another. Unlike a local array, a vector never holds garbage.
  • The size can be a variable: int n; cin >> n; vector<int> f(n); is fine. It is not for an array.

Member functions

A vector is an object with its own member functions: functions that belong to it and are called with a dot, the way you called cin.get() and cin.ignore().

CallWhat it does
v.push_back(x)Adds a new last element holding x. The size grows by 1.
v.pop_back()Removes the last element. The size shrinks by 1.
v.size()Returns the number of elements right now.
v.empty()Returns true if there are no elements.
v.clear()Removes every element. The size becomes 0.
v.resize(n)Changes the size to n. New elements are 0. Extra ones are removed.
v.at(i)The element at subscript i, with a check (see below).

Watch them work on one vector:

StatementContents aftersize()empty()
vector<int> s;(none)0true
s.push_back(8);81false
s.push_back(3);8 32false
s.push_back(5);8 3 53false
s.pop_back();8 32false
s.resize(4);8 3 0 04false
s.clear();(none)0true

push_back always adds at the end and pop_back always removes from the end, so you never need to know the size to use them. empty() returns a bool, which cout prints as 1 for true and 0 for false.

Reaching elements: [ ] and at()

v[i] works exactly as it does for an array. Subscripts run from 0 to size() - 1, and there is no checking, so a bad subscript is undefined behavior.

v.at(i) reaches the same element but checks i first. If i is out of range, at throws an exception: an error signal that stops the program with a message (here, out_of_range), unless the program has code to handle it. Handling exceptions is a later topic. The point now: with at, a bad subscript is caught the moment it happens instead of quietly damaging memory.

vector<int> v = {4, 5};
cout << v[1];       // 5
cout << v.at(1);    // 5, same element
cout << v.at(5);    // stops the program: out_of_range

The trap: a subscript never adds an element

vector<int> v;      // empty
v[0] = 5;           // BUG: there is no v[0]

A subscript only reaches an element that already exists. It never makes the vector bigger. This vector has no elements, so v[0] = 5; writes to memory that is not part of it: undefined behavior, with no error reported. To add a value, use v.push_back(5);. Or give the vector a size first: vector<int> v(1); and then v[0] = 5; is fine. (Python behaves the same way here: you cannot assign to lst[0] of an empty list, you must append. Python reports the error, C++ does not.)

Loops over a vector

The range-based for loop works on a vector, with the same rule as for arrays: a plain range variable is a copy, and & makes it refer to the real element.

vector<int> v = {2, 5, 7};
for (int &x : v)
    x = x + 1;              // v is now 3 6 8
for (int x : v)
    cout << x << " ";       // prints 3 6 8

Without the & in the first loop, only copies would change and the output would be 2 5 7.

A counting loop uses size() for its limit: for (int i = 0; i < v.size(); i++). size() returns an unsigned type, a whole-number type that cannot be negative. g++ with -Wall warns that this compares an int with an unsigned value. The loop still works. Just never compare size() with a negative number: -1 < v.size() is false, because -1 is converted to a huge unsigned value.

What vectors can do that arrays cannot

  • Copy with =. q = p; copies every element. Afterwards q is a separate vector, so changing q[0] does not change p[0].
  • Compare with ==. p == q is true when the two vectors have the same size and the same values in the same order.
  • Know their own size. A function that receives a vector can call size(), so no separate size parameter is needed, and a range-based for loop works inside the function.
  • Be returned from a function.

One difference catches people out. A vector passed to an ordinary parameter, void f(vector<int> v), is passed by value: the function gets a copy, unlike an array. To let the function change the caller's vector, use a reference parameter: void f(vector<int> &v). To only read it without making a copy, use const vector<int> &v.

Mistakes students make

  • Forgetting #include <vector>.
  • Mixing up vector<int> v(5); (five zeros) and vector<int> v = {5}; (one 5).
  • Using v[0] = x; on an empty vector instead of v.push_back(x);.
  • Thinking v[i] is checked. Only v.at(i) is.
  • Thinking pop_back removes the first element, or that clear sets the elements to 0. Both remove elements.
  • Calling a vector an associative container. It is a sequence container.
  • Expecting a function with a plain vector<int> v parameter to change the caller's vector.

What to remember for the test

  • #include <vector>, then vector<type> name;.
  • v(n): n elements of 0. v(n, x): n copies of x. = {a, b, c}: those values.
  • push_back adds at the end, pop_back removes the last, clear removes all, size counts, empty is true when size is 0.
  • v[i] is unchecked. v.at(i) checks and throws an exception if i is out of range.
  • A vector can change size while the program runs. An array cannot.
  • The STL has sequence containers (by position, such as vector) and associative containers (by key).

questions.prompt: Which statement defines an array of 12 doubles named sales?
questions.explain:
An array definition has three parts, in this order: the element type, the name, then the number of elements in square brackets. So `double sales[12];` makes 12 doubles, `sales[0]` to `sales[11]`.

The tempting wrong choice is `double sales(12);`. It compiles, but parentheses after a name give a starting value, so it makes one double that holds 12. `double[12] sales;` puts the brackets on the type instead of after the name, which C++ does not allow. `sales double[12];` puts the name first, so the compiler does not know what `sales` is.

questions.prompt: For the definition `int data[8];` which range lists every valid subscript?
questions.explain:
Subscripts start at 0, so the 8 elements are numbered 0 through 7. The last valid subscript is always the size minus 1.

"0 through 8" lists nine positions: `data[8]` is one past the end. "1 through 8" counts the way people do, but it misses `data[0]`, the first element, and includes `data[8]`, which is outside the array. "1 through 7" misses `data[0]` and covers only seven elements.

questions.prompt: In the definition `int hours[20];` the 20 is called the size ________.
questions.explain: The answer is declarator. In a definition the number in brackets says how many elements to make, and it is called the size declarator: `int hours[20];` makes 20 ints. The same brackets in a later statement, such as `hours[3] = 40;`, hold a subscript instead, which picks one element.

questions.prompt: In standard C++, the size declarator of an array must be a constant expression, so a variable that holds a value typed by the user cannot be used.
questions.explain:
True. The compiler must know how many elements an array has while it translates the program, before anyone types anything. So the size declarator has to be a constant expression: a literal like `10`, a named constant like `const int SIZE = 10;`, or arithmetic made only from those.

A variable filled by `cin >> n` gets its value only while the program runs, so `int a[n];` is not standard C++. g++ accepts it anyway as an extension, which is why it may work on your machine, but the test follows the standard.

questions.prompt: Given the lines below, which array definition is NOT allowed in standard C++?
questions.explain:
Ask of each size: can the compiler know this value before the program runs?

`int d[10];` uses a literal, so yes. `M` is a `const int` set to the literal 5, so it is a constant and `int a[M];` is fine. `M + 3` is arithmetic on constants, a fixed 8, so `int b[M + 3];` is fine too.

`n` is an ordinary variable. Even though it starts at 5, it is not a constant, so `int c[n];` is not allowed in standard C++. g++ accepts it as an extension and only warns with `-pedantic`, which is why it can look fine when you run it.
questions.code:
int n = 5;
const int M = 5;

questions.prompt: C++ automatically checks at run time that every array subscript is within the array and stops the program if it is not.
questions.explain:
False. C++ does no bounds checking. If a program uses a subscript outside the array, such as `a[10]` for a 10-element array, the code compiles, and at run time the program reads or writes the memory where that element would be.

That is undefined behavior: it may change another variable, crash, or seem to work. Nothing stops the program. Python would raise an IndexError, but C++ leaves it to the programmer to keep subscripts in range.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Trace the array line by line, always using the newest values.
```
start               v = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}
v[1] = v[3] + 1     v[3] is 40, so v[1] = 41
v[4] = v[1] - v[0]  uses the NEW v[1]: 41 - 10 = 31
```
`v[2]` is never assigned, so it still holds 30. The output is `41 31 30`.

The usual slips: using the old `v[1]` (20) in the second line, which gives 10, or counting subscripts from 1, which reads `v[3]` as 30.

questions.prompt: What is true about this loop?
choices: The compiler rejects it because 6 is not a valid subscript
The array grows to 7 elements automatically
The loop runs 6 times and is correct
It compiles, but the last pass stores to a[6], outside the array, which is undefined behavior
questions.explain:
List the values of i. The test `i <= 6` lets i be 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, so the loop runs 7 times. The array has 6 elements, subscripts 0 to 5, so the last pass stores into `a[6]`, which is outside the array. C++ does not check, so this compiles and is undefined behavior.

The compiler does not reject it: i is a variable, and C++ never checks subscripts. The array cannot grow, because its size is fixed when it is defined. And the loop does not run 6 times, it runs 7. The correct test is `i < 6`.

questions.prompt: In the two lines `int a[5];` and `a[5] = 9;` the number 5 has the same meaning both times.
questions.explain:
False. In `int a[5];` the 5 is the size declarator: the array has five elements. In `a[5] = 9;` the 5 is a subscript: it names one element.

The five elements are `a[0]` to `a[4]`, so `a[5]` is one past the end. That second line compiles, but it writes outside the array, which is undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: Using the array below, which subscript holds the value 45?
questions.explain:
Count from 0, not 1:
```
subscript:   0    1    2    3    4
value:      15   25   35   45   55
```
So 45 is at subscript 3. The empty brackets in `int a[]` only tell the compiler to count the list, which gives 5 elements. Answering 4 means counting positions the human way, starting at 1.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
The list `{4, 8}` has only two values for six elements. The listed values fill the front, and every element without a value is set to 0.
```
subscript:  0  1  2  3  4  5
a:          4  8  0  0  0  0
```
The loop prints each element followed by a space: `4 8 0 0 0 0`. The zeros are guaranteed because the array has a list. With no list at all, a local array would hold garbage instead.

questions.prompt: How many elements does q have?
choices: The definition is an error without a size
questions.explain:
When the brackets are empty, the compiler counts the values in the initialization list and makes that many elements. `{3, 6, 9, 12, 15}` has five values, so q has 5 elements, `q[0]` to `q[4]`.

4 is the last subscript, not the number of elements. 6 adds an extra element at the end, as if a null character were added. Only a string literal in double quotes gets that extra element, never a list of ints. And leaving out the size is legal whenever an initialization list is given.

questions.prompt: Which definition is an error?
questions.explain:
An initialization list may be shorter than the array but never longer. `int a[3] = {1, 2, 3, 4};` tries to put four values into three elements, so it does not compile.

The others are legal. `int b[5] = {1, 2};` is a partial list, so b holds 1 2 0 0 0. `int c[] = {1, 2, 3};` lets the compiler count three elements. `int d[4] = {};` uses empty braces, which set every element to 0.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
In `for (int x : n)` the range variable x is a copy of each element, not the element itself.
```
pass 1   x = 1 (copy of n[0])   x becomes 10, then is discarded
pass 2   x = 2 (copy of n[1])   x becomes 20, then is discarded
pass 3   x = 3 (copy of n[2])   x becomes 30, then is discarded
pass 4   x = 4 (copy of n[3])   x becomes 40, then is discarded
```
The array is never touched, so the second loop prints the original values: `1 2 3 4`. The tempting answer 10 20 30 40 would need `int &x`, which makes x refer to the real element.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
The `&` in `int &x` makes x a reference: another name for the element itself, not a copy. So `x = x * 10` changes the array.
```
pass 1   x is n[0]   n[0] = 1 * 10 = 10
pass 2   x is n[1]   n[1] = 2 * 10 = 20
pass 3   x is n[2]   n[2] = 3 * 10 = 30
pass 4   x is n[3]   n[3] = 4 * 10 = 40
```
The second loop uses a plain copy, which is fine because it only prints. Output: `10 20 30 40`.

questions.prompt: Which loop doubles every element of the int array a in place?
questions.explain:
To change the elements themselves, the range variable must be a reference, so `for (int &x : a) x *= 2;` is right. On each pass x is another name for one element, and `x *= 2` doubles that element.

`for (int x : a) x *= 2;` compiles, but it doubles copies, so a is unchanged. `for (int x : a) a *= 2;` tries to multiply the whole array, which is not a number, so it does not compile. `for (x : a) x *= 2;` leaves out the type of the range variable, which is also a compile error.

questions.prompt: Write the range-based for header, using auto and a by-value loop variable named val, that visits each element of the array scores.
questions.explain: The header is `for (auto val : scores)`. The pattern is `for (type rangeVariable : array)`. Here the type is `auto`, so the compiler uses the element type of scores. The range variable is `val`, and a colon, not a semicolon, separates it from the array. With no `&`, val gets a copy of each element in turn. A full loop could be `for (auto val : scores) cout << val << " ";`.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
`auto [a, b, c] = p;` makes three new variables that hold copies of the elements.
```
a = 7, b = 8, c = 9    copies of p[0], p[1], p[2]
b = b + 100            b is 108, p[1] is still 8
```
So the output is `7 108 9 8`. The tempting wrong answer ends in 108, which assumes b is tied to `p[1]`. It is not. Changing a copy never changes the array.

questions.prompt: What happens with this code?
choices: Compile error, because the number of names does not match the number of elements
x gets 1, y gets 2, and 3 is ignored
x gets 1, y gets 2, and the array shrinks
questions.explain:
A structured binding must list exactly one name per element. p has 3 elements but only two names are given, so the compiler rejects the line.

C++ does not quietly ignore the extra value, it does not shift values around (so y could never get 3), and an array's size never changes. To unpack this array you would write `auto [x, y, z] = p;`, which gives x 1, y 2 and z 3.

questions.prompt: The special character with ASCII value 0 that marks the end of a C-string is called the ________ character.
questions.explain: The answer is null. The null character is written `'\0'` and has ASCII code 0. A C-string stores text in a char array and puts `'\0'` right after the last real character, so code such as `cout` knows where the text stops. For example, `char w[] = "hi";` holds 'h', 'i' and '\0'. It is not the digit '0', which has code 48.

questions.prompt: A char array is defined as `char w[] = "plum";`. How many elements does w have, and what does w[4] hold?
choices: 4 elements; w[4] is out of range
5 elements; w[4] holds the null character
4 elements; w[3] holds the null character
questions.explain:
A string literal in double quotes always gets a null character added at the end. So "plum" needs its 4 letters plus `'\0'`:
```
subscript:  0    1    2    3    4
w:         'p'  'l'  'u'  'm'  '\0'
```
That is 5 elements, and `w[4]` holds the null. "4 elements" forgets the null. "w[4] holds 'm'" counts from 1, but 'm' is at subscript 3. And `w[4]` is not out of range, because the array has 5 elements.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
First the loop adds up the elements:
```
i=0   s = 0 + 4   = 4
i=1   s = 4 + 9   = 13
i=2   s = 13 + 2  = 15
i=3   s = 15 + 7  = 22
```
`s / 4` has an int on both sides, so it is integer division and the fraction is dropped: 5. In `s / 4.0` the 4.0 is a double, so the division keeps the fraction: 5.5. The output is `22 5 5.5`. Printing 5.5 in the middle is the common mistake: it takes only one double to get a fractional result, and that division has none.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Trace the running highest value:
```
start          hi = 12, pos = 0
i=1  40 > 12   yes   hi = 40, pos = 1
i=2   7 > 40   no
i=3  40 > 40   no    equal is not greater
i=4  25 > 40   no
```
The output is `40 1`. The tempting answer is 40 3, which assumes the second 40 replaces the first. With strict `>`, an equal value never passes the test, so the first of the tied highest values keeps its position.

questions.prompt: What does this print? (Note the operator.)
questions.explain:
Same data as the `>` version, but now an equal value also passes:
```
start           hi = 12, pos = 0
i=1  40 >= 12   yes   hi = 40, pos = 1
i=2   7 >= 40   no
i=3  40 >= 40   yes   hi = 40, pos = 3
i=4  25 >= 40   no
```
The output is `40 3`. Because 40 >= 40 is true, the later tie overwrites pos, so the last of the equal highest values wins. With `>` the answer would be 40 1.

questions.prompt: Two int arrays of the same size, a and b, hold identical values. What does `if (a == b)` do?
choices: It compares every element and is true
It compares only the first elements
It compares the addresses of the arrays, so it is false
questions.explain:
An array name with no brackets stands for the memory address where the array begins. So `a == b` asks whether a and b start at the same place in memory. Two separate arrays never do, so the test is false even though every value matches.

It is not a compile error (g++ only gives a warning). It does not look at the elements at all, not every element and not even the first one. To compare contents, use a loop: set `bool same = true;` and make it false whenever `a[i] != b[i]`.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Each pass copies the element on its left into the current position. From the second pass on, that left element has already been overwritten with 1 by the pass before.
```
start   1 2 3 4 5
i=1     a[1] = a[0], which is 1    1 1 3 4 5
i=2     a[2] = a[1], which is 1    1 1 1 4 5
i=3     a[3] = a[2], which is 1    1 1 1 1 5
i=4     a[4] = a[3], which is 1    1 1 1 1 1
```
The output is `1 1 1 1 1`. The tempting output, 1 1 2 3 4, is what a shift to the right should give, but that needs the loop to run backwards from the end, so each value is read before it is overwritten.

questions.prompt: Which code correctly copies the 8-element int array src into the 8-element int array dst?
choices: for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) dst[i] = src[i];
for (int i = 0; i <= 8; i++) dst[i] = src[i];
questions.explain:
C++ cannot assign one array to another, so you copy the elements one by one. `for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) dst[i] = src[i];` visits subscripts 0 to 7, every element exactly once.

`dst = src;` does not compile. `dst[8] = src[8];` copies a single element, and subscript 8 is past the end of both arrays. The loop with `i <= 8` copies all 8 elements and then makes one more pass with i equal to 8, outside both arrays, which is an off-by-one error.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
`d[count++] = value;` stores at the current value of count, then adds 1 to count.
```
d[count++] = 6    d[0] = 6, count becomes 1
d[count++] = 2    d[1] = 2, count becomes 2
d[count++] = 9    d[2] = 9, count becomes 3
```
The loop runs while `i < count`, so it sums only `d[0]` to `d[2]`: 6 + 2 + 9 = 17. The output is `3 17`. The other five elements were never given values, which is why the loop must stop at count and not at 8.

questions.prompt: An array that is defined large enough for the maximum but currently holds fewer values, with a separate counter, is called a ________ filled array.
questions.explain: The answer is partially. A partially filled array is defined at the largest size the program might need, but only the first few elements hold real data. A separate int, often named count, says how many are in use. With count equal to 3, elements 0, 1 and 2 hold data, and every loop over the array runs `i < count`, not to the full size.

questions.prompt: All the values in the int array vals are positive. A student finds the smallest value with `int lo = 0;` and then `if (vals[i] < lo) lo = vals[i];` inside a loop over the array. What is the result?
choices: It correctly finds the smallest value
lo stays 0, which is wrong, because 0 is smaller than every element
It finds the smallest value except the first element
questions.explain:
Trace it with any positive values, for example 5, 3 and 8. lo starts at 0. Is 5 < 0? No. Is 3 < 0? No. Is 8 < 0? No. No positive number is less than 0, so lo never changes, and the program reports 0 as the smallest value even though 0 is not in the array.

It does not find the largest value, because the test is `<`. It does not just miss the first element: it misses every element. The fix is to start with `int lo = vals[0];`, a value that really is in the array.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
The loop compares the two arrays position by position and counts the positions that differ:
```
i=0   1 vs 1   same
i=1   2 vs 9   different   diff = 1
i=2   3 vs 3   same
i=3   4 vs 0   different   diff = 2
```
The output is `2`. This element-by-element loop is the right way to compare arrays. `a == b` would only compare their memory addresses.

questions.prompt: An array r of 100 ints currently holds 37 valid readings, and count is 37. Which loop displays only the valid readings?
choices: for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) cout << r[i] << ' ';
for (int i = 0; i <= count; i++) cout << r[i] << ' ';
for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) cout << r[i] << ' ';
for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) cout << r[i] << ' ';
questions.explain:
The 37 valid readings are in `r[0]` to `r[36]`. So the loop must start at 0 and stop before count: `for (int i = 0; i < count; i++)`.

Running to 100 also prints the 63 unused elements, which are not valid readings. `i <= count` prints `r[37]`, one unused element too many. Starting at 1 skips `r[0]`, the first reading.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
best holds a subscript, not a score. Trace it:
```
start                        best = 0   (pts[0] is 70)
i=1   pts[1] 95 > pts[0] 70?  yes   best = 1
i=2   pts[2] 88 > pts[1] 95?  no    best stays 1
```
After the loop best is 1, so the program prints `name[1]` and `pts[1]`: `Bo 95`. The same subscript picks the matching name out of the other array, which is the whole point of parallel arrays.

questions.prompt: Which best describes parallel arrays?
choices: Two arrays that must have the same data type
Arrays stored next to each other in memory
Two or more arrays whose elements with the same subscript hold related data
questions.explain:
Parallel arrays are linked by subscript: element k of each array describes the same item, so `name[2]` and `score[2]` are both about one student.

They do not need the same data type. A string array of names with an int array of scores is the usual case. "An array with two subscripts" describes a two-dimensional array, which is a different thing. And "parallel" says nothing about where the arrays sit in memory. C++ does not even know the arrays are related.

questions.prompt: Parallel arrays must all have the same data type.
questions.explain: False. Parallel arrays are tied together by subscript, not by type. The usual example mixes types: a string array of names and an int array of scores, where `name[i]` and `score[i]` describe the same person. What they do need is the same number of elements, with the items in the same order.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
Search id for 309, then use the same subscript in price.
```
i=0   101 == 309?  no
i=1   205 == 309?  no
i=2   309 == 309?  yes   found = 2
i=3   412 == 309?  no
```
found is 2, and `price[2]` is 6.25, so the output is `2 6.25`. The loop does not stop at the match, but there is only one 309, so found stays 2. If 309 were missing, found would stay -1 and `price[-1]` would be outside the array, which is why real code checks `found != -1` first.

questions.prompt: The arrays item and cost are parallel. A program swaps item[0] and item[1] but does nothing to cost. What is the effect?
choices: Two items now show the wrong cost
Nothing, because the arrays are independent
questions.explain:
C++ has no idea that item and cost belong together. The link exists only in how the program uses subscripts. After the swap, `item[0]` holds what used to be `item[1]`, but `cost[0]` still holds the old `cost[0]`. So those two items are each paired with the other's cost.

For example, with items pen and pad costing 1.25 and 3.50, after swapping only item, pad shows 1.25 and pen shows 3.50. The code compiles and runs with no error, and cost is not swapped automatically. Saying nothing happens because the arrays are independent gets it backwards: they are independent as far as C++ knows, and that is exactly why swapping one leaves the other out of step. The fix is to make the same swap in cost.

questions.prompt: Parallel arrays are linked by using the same ________ in each array.
questions.explain: The answer is subscript. In parallel arrays the same subscript picks related data in every array: `name[3]` and `score[3]` describe the same student. A loop uses one subscript variable, i, for all the arrays, so each name stays lined up with its own score.

questions.prompt: When an array name is used as a function argument, what does the function receive?
choices: The memory address of the first element
A copy of the first element only
questions.explain:
When an array's name is used as an argument, C++ passes the memory address of its first element. The function uses that address to reach the caller's own elements, so any change it makes is a real change.

Nothing is copied: not every element, and not just the first one. The number of elements is not passed either, which is why array functions take a separate size parameter.

questions.prompt: Arrays are passed to functions by value, so the function always works on its own copy.
questions.explain: False. A single variable is passed by value unless you use a reference, but an array is not passed by value. The function receives the address of the array's first element and works directly on the caller's elements, so `a[0] = 5;` inside the function changes the caller's array. Only a single element passed on its own, such as `f(v[0])` to an int parameter, is copied.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
bump receives the address of v, so a and v are the same three elements.
```
i=0   a[0] += 10   v[0] goes from 1 to 11
i=1   a[1] += 10   v[1] goes from 2 to 12
i=2   a[2] += 10   v[2] goes from 3 to 13
```
Back in main, v holds the changed values, so the output is `11 12 13`. Answering 1 2 3 assumes the function worked on a copy, but arrays are never passed by value.

questions.prompt: Which is a correct header for a function that only reads an int array and also receives the number of elements?
choices: void show(const int a, int n)
void show(const int a[], int n)
questions.explain:
An array parameter is written as the type, the name, then empty brackets: `int a[]`. `const` in front promises the function will only read it. The size is a separate parameter with its own type. So `void show(const int a[], int n)` is right.

`void show(int a[], n)` gives n no type, which is a compile error. `void show(const int a, int n)` has no brackets, so a is a single int and an array could not be passed to it. `void show(int[] a, int n)` puts the brackets before the name, which is Java style, not C++.
